claim_verdicts.evidence: db/seed.sql@stage-0 inserts orders with ids 1-12 and payments whose order_id values are 1,2,3,5,7,8,10,11 — eight distinct order_ids, so no order carries two payment rows. customers holds ids 1-5 and id 5 occurs in no orders row. customers LEFT JOIN orders LEFT JOIN payments therefore yields 12 order rows plus one NULL-extended row = 13. Not executed: docker version fails here (open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine: The system cannot find the file specified), so this is inspection of the fixed seed data at the tag, which is deterministic.

db/seed.sql@stage-0: customers row (1, 'Trần Minh Anh', ...); orders (1,1,...), (2,1,...), (10,1,...) all carry customer_id 1; payments (1, 1, ..., 2150000, 'card'), (2, 2, ..., 890000, 'card'), (7, 10, ..., 1730000, 'card'). Exactly the three amounts §2 asks the reader to add, and they total 4770000, the figure §5 prints for him.

PostgreSQL 17 §9.21, Table 9.60 General-Purpose Aggregate Functions lists all five: "count ( * ) → bigint — Computes the number of input rows."; "sum ( integer ) → bigint — Computes the sum of the non-null input values."; "avg — Computes the average (arithmetic mean) of all the non-null input values."; "min ( see text ) — Computes the minimum of the non-null input values."; "max ( see text ) — Computes the maximum of the non-null input values."

PostgreSQL 17, Table 9.60: "count ( * ) → bigint — Computes the number of input rows." and "count ( "any" ) → bigint — Computes the number of input rows in which the input value is not null." That is exactly the split §3 states and §5 applies to count(*) versus count(p.id).

PostgreSQL 17, Conditional Expressions: "The COALESCE function returns the first of its arguments that is not null. Null is returned only if all arguments are null." §3's wording ("a function returning its first argument that is not NULL") matches, and coalesce(sum(p.amount_vnd), 0) in the quoted query is that case.

PostgreSQL 17 SELECT, Description, numbered processing order: "2. All elements in the FROM list are computed… 3. If the WHERE clause is specified, all rows that do not satisfy the condition are eliminated… 4. If the GROUP BY clause is specified… the output is combined into groups… and the results of aggregate functions are computed. If the HAVING clause is present, it eliminates groups that do not satisfy the given condition… 8. If the ORDER BY clause is specified, the returned rows are sorted." The claim's second half disclaims rather than asserts server behaviour.

PostgreSQL 17 tutorial 2.7: "WHERE selects input rows before groups and aggregates are computed (thus, it controls which rows go into the aggregate computation), whereas HAVING selects group rows after groups and aggregates are computed." and "Thus, the WHERE clause must not contain aggregate functions; it makes no sense to try to use an aggregate to determine which rows will be inputs to the aggregates." The docs state the prohibition; they quote no error text, and the claim asserts only rejection. No live run (Docker daemon unreachable).

PostgreSQL 17 §7.2.3: "The GROUP BY clause is used to group together those rows in a table that have the same values in all the columns listed." and "The effect is to combine each set of rows having common values into one group row that represents all rows in the group." Table 9.60 defines each aggregate over its input rows, which after grouping are the rows of the group.

PostgreSQL 17 SELECT, GROUP BY: "it is not valid for the SELECT list expressions to refer to ungrouped columns except within aggregate functions or when the ungrouped column is functionally dependent on the grouped columns… A functional dependency exists if the grouped columns (or a subset thereof) are the primary key of the table containing the ungrouped column." The same page adds that PostgreSQL recognizes functional dependency only when a table's primary key is in the GROUP BY list — so §4's "one relaxation" is right for 17.

PostgreSQL 17 §7.2.3: "the HAVING clause can be used, much like a WHERE clause, to eliminate groups from the result" and "Expressions in the HAVING clause can refer both to grouped expressions and to ungrouped expressions (which necessarily involve an aggregate function)." SELECT ref: each referenced column "must unambiguously reference a grouping column, unless the reference appears within an aggregate function". Tutorial 2.7: HAVING acts after groups and aggregates are computed.

ORDER BY paid_vnd DESC, c.id gives exactly 6400000, 4870000, 4770000, 3150000, 0 and five rows, with no ties to make the order ambiguous. Inspection only, no run: the Docker daemon is unreachable on this machine.

db/seed.sql@stage-0: customer 2 owns orders 3, 4 and 11; payments exist for order 3 (3520000, 'bank_transfer') and order 11 (1350000, 'cod') but not for order 4. The LEFT JOIN keeps order 4 with p.id NULL, so count(*) = 3 and count(p.id) = 2 per Table 9.60's count("any") definition. Matches §5's "rows_in_group 3 and payments_made 2".

db/seed.sql@stage-0: customer 5 ('Vũ Gia Khánh') appears in no orders row, so customers LEFT JOIN orders emits one NULL-extended row for him and the second LEFT JOIN keeps it: count(*)=1, count(p.id)=0, sum(p.amount_vnd)=NULL, coalesce(...,0)=0. An INNER JOIN to orders would drop that row at the join step, before any group exists.

PostgreSQL 17 §9.21: "It should be noted that except for count, these functions return a null value when no rows are selected. In particular, sum of no rows returns null, not zero as one might expect." Same page: "All these functions ignore null values in their aggregated input" and sum "Computes the sum of the non-null input values" — so a group whose only value is NULL has no non-null input and yields null too, which is Vũ Gia Khánh's case.

Card payments at stage-0: 2150000 (order 1, c1), 890000 (order 2, c1), 1730000 (order 10, c1), 2140000 (order 7, c3). With both INNER JOINs and WHERE p.method='card' the groups are Trần Minh Anh 4770000 and Lê Quốc Dũng 2140000; both clear HAVING > 2000000, so two rows, sorted DESC. His first-query total is 1010000 (payment 4, 'cod', order 5) + 2140000 = 3150000, a difference of exactly 1010000. Inspection only; no Docker daemon to run it.

db/seed.sql@stage-0: orders 3 and 11 carry customer_id 2 and their payments are (3,…,3520000,'bank_transfer') and (8,…,1350000,'cod'). Customer 4 owns orders 8, 9 and 12; payments name order_ids 1,2,3,5,7,8,10,11, so only order 8 matches — (6, 8, …, 6400000, 'bank_transfer') is her only payment. Neither customer has a 'card' row, so after the INNER JOINs (2 rows for c2, 1 for c4) WHERE removes every one and no group is formed for either.

PostgreSQL 17 SELECT. ORDER BY: "Each expression can be the name or ordinal number of an output column (SELECT list item), or… an arbitrary expression formed from input-column values." GROUP BY: an expression "can be an input column name, or the name or ordinal number of an output column". HAVING: "condition is the same as specified for the WHERE clause", and each referenced column "must unambiguously reference a grouping column, unless the reference appears within an aggregate function". HAVING is granted no output name — documented by contrast, not by an explicit ban; no run was possible.

PostgreSQL 17 SELECT, HAVING: "Each column referenced in condition must unambiguously reference a grouping column, unless the reference appears within an aggregate function or the ungrouped column is functionally dependent on the grouping columns." The second query groups by c.full_name only; payments.method is not grouped, not inside an aggregate, and not functionally dependent (dependency requires the grouped columns to be payments' primary key), so the condition is rejected.

PostgreSQL 17 §7.2.3: "In general, if a table is grouped, columns that are not listed in GROUP BY cannot be referenced except in aggregate expressions." SELECT/GROUP BY: "A functional dependency exists if the grouped columns (or a subset thereof) are the primary key of the table containing the ungrouped column." The first query groups c.id, c.full_name — customers' primary key (db/schema.sql l.12), not orders' — so o.status is neither grouped, nor aggregated, nor functionally dependent, and the query is rejected. §6 asserts rejection only, no error text.

psql 17 reference, title line: "psql — PostgreSQL interactive terminal"; \pset footer: "it must be either on or off which will enable or disable display of the table footer (the (n rows) count)" — the footer is on by default and --no-psqlrc in the script rules out a user override. scripts/sql/run-query.sh@stage-0 l.7-11: query="${1:-select-basics}" then psql --host db --username donhang --dbname donhang --no-psqlrc --echo-queries --set ON_ERROR_STOP=on --file "/repo/db/queries/${query}.sql".

Line 23 of db/queries/revenue-by-customer.sql is indeed "HAVING sum(p.amount_vnd) > 2000000". Card totals at stage-0 are 4770000 (Trần Minh Anh) and 2140000 (Lê Quốc Dũng), so a threshold of 3000000 keeps one group. The first query (l.5-14) is a separate statement with no threshold, hence unchanged. Two inferences, not runs: psql prints the singular "(1 row)" footer, and the edit behaves as the arithmetic says — the Docker daemon is unreachable, so nothing was executed.

PostgreSQL 17 §7.2.2: "each row of the derived virtual table is checked against the search condition. If the result of the condition is true, the row is kept in the output table, otherwise (i.e., if the result is false or null) it is discarded." §9.2: "Ordinary comparison operators yield null (signifying "unknown"), not true or false, when either input is null." So p.method = 'card' over a NULL p.method yields null and WHERE discards that row, exactly as quiz q5's explanation b says.
